doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Wartime boyhood expectations and his father's anti-war views
summary: As a boy he feared the war would end before he could fight; his father was anti-war.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well it wasn’t a concern. When I was 14 years old I was afraid the war would be over before I could get into it. You know, I was a kid. I wanted to be a glory boy, I wanted to fly airplanes, I wanted whatever it was. Because you remember, I was brought up on World War I pop literature. You were always reading — you remember World War I, during the thirties, when I was a kid, reading comic books and reading magazines and reading just kids books and whatever, the war that you read about was the first World War and the brave marines at The Somme or whatever it was, and the Red Baron flying the airplanes and so forth. So that was the romance of the war, it was sort of part of what you grew up with if you were a boy in my generation. Now my father was very anti-war of course, and he was always talking about the merchants of death and so forth, because they were all left wing and hated all of this and they were older and had actually known what the war was about. So for me, and then by the time I got to be a senior in high school, or a junior and senior in high school, it was clear that the war was going to be over. We knew that that was a dead issue. And so the likelihood of fighting, there were some of my friends who were just enough older, did get drafted and served in what they called the Constabulate. They were occupation forces in Germany and some in Japan and whatever. So I never particularly worried about that so I didn’t think I was going to go. We didn’t know there was going to be a Korean conflict.
